name: Bitcoin
summary: The first cryptocurrency network: a proof-of-work blockchain for sending and holding bitcoin (BTC) without a central operator.
goodToKnow: Bitcoin's scripting language is deliberately limited; it does not run general-purpose smart contracts the way Ethereum does.
"Bitcoin" can mean the network/protocol or the BTC currency unit; Bitcoin Core is the main software implementation, not the network itself.

name: Ethereum
summary: Proof-of-stake blockchain that runs smart contracts on the EVM; it also serves as the settlement layer for many rollups.
goodToKnow: Ethereum switched from proof of work to proof of stake in September 2022 ("the Merge").
ETH is the native asset used to pay transaction fees (gas); "Ethereum" is the network.
Many L2 rollups post their data and proofs to Ethereum, which is why it sits at the centre of the Ethereum ecosystem.

name: Solana
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain designed for high throughput, running transactions in parallel with its own virtual machine (SVM).
goodToKnow: Transactions declare in advance which accounts they read and write, which lets the runtime execute non-conflicting ones in parallel.
Solana programs are not EVM contracts: Ethereum tools and addresses do not work there directly.
The network has had several full outages in the past (between 2021 and 2024).

name: BNB Chain
summary: Blockchain ecosystem started by Binance; its main network, BNB Smart Chain, is an EVM-compatible chain paying fees in BNB.
goodToKnow: BNB Smart Chain uses a small, permissioned-by-stake validator set (Proof of Staked Authority), trading decentralisation for low fees and speed.
BNB Chain also includes opBNB (an L2) and BNB Greenfield (storage); the older BNB Beacon Chain was shut down in 2024.
Many tokens on BNB Smart Chain are "Binance-Peg" versions of assets from other chains, issued by Binance rather than the original issuer.

name: Avalanche
summary: Proof-of-stake network of interoperable chains; its C-Chain runs EVM smart contracts and others can launch their own Avalanche L1s.
goodToKnow: The primary network has three chains: C-Chain (smart contracts), X-Chain (asset transfers) and P-Chain (validators and L1 management).
"Subnets" were renamed "Avalanche L1s" in the Avalanche9000 upgrade (December 2024); older articles use the old name.

name: Cardano
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain using the Ouroboros protocol and an extended UTXO model for its native ADA and smart contracts.
goodToKnow: Cardano uses an extended UTXO (eUTXO) model, closer to Bitcoin's than to Ethereum's account model, so contracts are written differently.
Its protocol design is developed through peer-reviewed research, and on-chain governance (CIP-1694) lets ADA holders vote on changes.

name: IOTA
summary: Layer-1 network that started as a DAG "Tangle" ledger and, since its 2025 Rebased upgrade, is a validator-run proof-of-stake chain.
goodToKnow: The "Rebased" upgrade (mainnet 5 May 2025) replaced the original Tangle design. The hub's DAG demo shows that historical Tangle design, not today's IOTA.
As of November 2026: an object-based ledger with Move smart contracts, run by a delegated proof-of-stake validator committee using Starfish consensus.
Starfish (enabled on mainnet in 2026) succeeds Mysticeti; it is a DAG-based protocol among validators, unlike the old Tangle of user transactions.

name: Cosmos Hub
summary: Proof-of-stake blockchain at the centre of the Cosmos ecosystem, connected to other Cosmos SDK chains through IBC.
goodToKnow: "Cosmos" usually means the whole ecosystem of independent chains built with the Cosmos SDK; the Cosmos Hub is just one of them.
Its native token is ATOM; the Hub's node software is called Gaia.

name: Osmosis
summary: Cosmos SDK blockchain built around a decentralised exchange (AMM) for swapping tokens that arrive from other chains over IBC.
goodToKnow: App-chain: a blockchain built for one application, with its own validators.
Osmosis is the name of both the chain and the exchange running on it; OSMO is its native token.

name: dYdX Chain
summary: Cosmos SDK blockchain dedicated to trading perpetual futures, with its order book run by the chain's validators.
goodToKnow: App-chain: a blockchain built for one application, with its own validators.
Earlier dYdX versions (v3 and before) ran on Ethereum and an Ethereum L2; dYdX Chain ("v4") is a separate network.

name: Polkadot
summary: Proof-of-stake network whose relay chain provides shared security to connected chains (parachains) that exchange messages via XCM.
goodToKnow: Polkadot Hub (the system chain for assets and smart contracts) enabled smart contracts on mainnet in January 2026.
Kusama is a separate, faster-moving sister network often used to try features before Polkadot.
DOT is used for staking, governance and fees.

name: Monero
summary: Proof-of-work cryptocurrency designed for private payments, hiding the sender, receiver and amount of every transaction.
goodToKnow: Privacy is on by default: ring signatures hide the sender, stealth addresses hide the receiver and RingCT hides amounts, which is why on-chain tracing stops there.
Because of this, some exchanges have delisted XMR or restrict it in certain jurisdictions.
A planned upgrade (FCMP++) would replace ring signatures; as of November 2026 no mainnet date has been set.

name: Lightning Network
summary: Payment network on top of Bitcoin that uses payment channels so users can send many small, fast payments off-chain.
goodToKnow: Only opening and closing a channel are Bitcoin transactions; payments in between are exchanged off-chain and routed through other nodes.
Receiving usually requires being online (or using a service that is), and a channel's capacity limits how much can move through it.
Lightning is not a rollup: it does not post transaction batches to Bitcoin.

name: Arbitrum One
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup that runs transactions off-chain and posts their data to Ethereum, with fraud proofs to settle disputes.
goodToKnow: Optimistic: results are assumed valid unless challenged, so native withdrawals to Ethereum take about a week.
"Arbitrum" also covers Arbitrum Nova (a separate chain) and the Orbit/Arbitrum chains framework used to launch other chains such as L3s.
Governed by the Arbitrum DAO (ARB token); the technology is developed mainly by Offchain Labs.

name: OP Mainnet
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup built with the OP Stack; it posts transaction data to Ethereum and uses fault proofs for withdrawals.
goodToKnow: "Optimism" is also the name of the foundation and of the Optimism Collective; OP Mainnet is the specific chain.
The OP Stack is open-source software used by other chains in the "Superchain"; Base, which launched on it, moved to its own stack in 2026.
Native withdrawals to Ethereum take about a week because of the challenge period.

name: Base
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup incubated by Coinbase; it runs transactions off-chain and settles them on Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Base launched on Optimism's OP Stack; with its Azul upgrade (mainnet 28 May 2026) it switched to its own base/base node software.
Base is operated by a company (Coinbase), which runs its sequencer; it is a separate network from the Coinbase exchange.
As of November 2026, Base combines TEE attestations and ZK proofs (since May 2026), so native withdrawals take about 1 to 5 days.

name: ZKsync Era
summary: Ethereum zk-rollup (validity rollup) that proves its batches to Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs; it is EVM-compatible.
goodToKnow: Validity proofs mean withdrawals do not need a week-long challenge period, though proof generation adds some delay.
Not to be confused with zkSync Lite, the earlier ZKsync rollup, which was deprecated in 2026.
Built with the ZK Stack, which other teams use to launch their own chains.

name: Starknet
summary: Ethereum validity rollup that uses STARK proofs; smart contracts are written in the Cairo language rather than for the EVM.
goodToKnow: Starknet is not EVM-compatible: Solidity contracts and Ethereum tooling need adaptation.
Every account on Starknet is a smart contract (native account abstraction).
Developed by StarkWare; STRK is the network token.

name: Linea
summary: Ethereum zk-rollup developed by Consensys that executes EVM transactions and proves them to Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs.
goodToKnow: Gas is paid in ETH, not in the LINEA token.
Developed by Consensys, the company behind MetaMask.

name: Scroll
summary: Ethereum zk-rollup that executes EVM transactions and proves them to Ethereum with zero-knowledge proofs.
goodToKnow: Aims for compatibility with Ethereum at the bytecode level, so most Ethereum contracts and tools work unchanged.
Gas is paid in ETH; SCR is the governance token.

name: ApeChain
summary: Arbitrum Orbit L3 for the ApeCoin ecosystem that settles on Arbitrum One and uses APE as its gas token.
goodToKnow: "L3" has no single agreed definition; here it means a chain that settles on an L2 rather than directly on Ethereum.
Settlement layer (as of November 2026): Arbitrum One. Data is normally kept by a data availability committee (AnyTrust) rather than posted in full.
Built for the ApeCoin community; APE is the token, ApeChain is the network.

name: Xai
summary: Gaming-focused Arbitrum Orbit L3 that settles on Arbitrum One and uses a data availability committee (AnyTrust).
goodToKnow: "L3" has no single agreed definition; here it means a chain that settles on an L2 rather than directly on Ethereum.
Settlement layer (as of November 2026): Arbitrum One.
Not related to xAI, the AI company; this Xai is a blockchain for games, with the XAI token.

name: Uniswap
summary: Decentralised exchange protocol where users swap tokens against liquidity pools priced by an automated market maker (AMM).
goodToKnow: "Uniswap" can mean the on-chain protocol, the Uniswap Labs web app, or the UNI governance token.
Liquidity providers can lose value versus holding (impermanent loss) when prices move.
Deployed on Ethereum and many L2s and other chains; each deployment has separate pools.

name: Aave
summary: Decentralised lending protocol where users deposit crypto to earn interest or borrow against collateral.
goodToKnow: Loans are over-collateralised; if collateral value falls too far, positions can be liquidated automatically.
Aave also issues its own stablecoin, GHO; AAVE is the governance token.
Runs as separate markets on Ethereum and several other networks.

name: Lido
summary: Liquid staking protocol for Ethereum: users stake ETH and receive stETH, a token that tracks their staked ETH and rewards.
goodToKnow: stETH is a claim on staked ETH; it can trade slightly away from 1 ETH on markets, and redemptions go through a withdrawal queue.
Staking is done by node operators chosen through Lido's governance; LDO is the governance token.
wstETH is a "wrapped" form of stETH whose balance does not change, used by many DeFi apps.

name: Sky (ex-MakerDAO)
summary: DeFi protocol issuing the USDS and DAI stablecoins against collateral; formerly MakerDAO, governed by SKY token holders.
goodToKnow: Formerly MakerDAO (rebranded to Sky in August 2024). DAI still exists and can be upgraded 1:1 to USDS; MKR can be upgraded to SKY.
Vault price feeds come mainly from Chronicle, an oracle network that grew out of Maker's oracle team and is now a separate project.
Users mint stablecoins by locking collateral in vaults; under-collateralised vaults are liquidated.

name: Curve
summary: Decentralised exchange whose AMM pools are designed for swapping similar-value assets, such as stablecoins, with low price impact.
goodToKnow: Its stableswap formula keeps prices tight while a pool is balanced; when one asset depegs, the pool fills up with it.
Curve also issues a stablecoin, crvUSD; CRV is the governance token.

name: Jupiter
summary: Swap aggregator on Solana that routes trades across many exchanges to find a price; it also offers other trading products.
goodToKnow: An aggregator does not hold liquidity itself; it splits and routes orders through other Solana DEXs.
JUP is its governance token.

name: USDC (Circle)
summary: Dollar stablecoin issued by Circle, redeemable 1:1 for US dollars and backed by cash and short-term US government assets.
goodToKnow: Centrally issued: Circle can freeze USDC held at specific addresses.
Issued natively on many blockchains; "bridged" USDC on some chains is a different token from Circle-issued USDC.
Temporarily lost its peg in March 2023 when part of its reserves was held at Silicon Valley Bank.

name: USDT (Tether)
summary: Dollar stablecoin issued by Tether, intended to be redeemable 1:1 for US dollars and backed by Tether's reserves.
goodToKnow: Centrally issued: Tether can freeze USDT held at specific addresses.
USDT on BNB Chain is a Binance-issued token ("Binance-Peg") backed by USDT that Binance holds, not a Tether issuance.
Tether publishes the list of chains it issues on; versions elsewhere are bridged or third-party tokens.

name: Coinbase
summary: Centralised exchange where users buy, sell and hold crypto with traditional money; it also incubated the Base network.
goodToKnow: Centralised exchange (custodial): Coinbase holds users' keys, so funds there are an account balance, not self-custody.
Coinbase's self-custody wallet app (originally Coinbase Wallet) is separate from exchange accounts.
Co-founded the Centre consortium with Circle that launched USDC in 2018.

name: Kraken
summary: Centralised exchange where users buy, sell and hold crypto with traditional money; founded in 2011.
goodToKnow: Centralised exchange (custodial): Kraken holds users' keys, so funds there are an account balance, not self-custody.
Like other exchanges, it can freeze accounts or funds, for example at law-enforcement request.
Kraken also backs Ink, an Ethereum L2 network.

name: Chainlink
summary: Oracle network that brings off-chain data, such as asset prices, onto blockchains; it also offers cross-chain messaging (CCIP).
goodToKnow: An oracle is needed because smart contracts cannot fetch outside data themselves.
Price feeds are produced by independent node operators and aggregated on-chain.
LINK is the token used to pay node operators.

name: Pyth
summary: Oracle network that publishes price data contributed directly by trading firms and exchanges, for use on many blockchains.
goodToKnow: Prices are "pulled": an application (or user) posts a fresh signed price on-chain when it needs one, instead of the oracle pushing updates.
Prices are aggregated on Pythnet, Pyth's own appchain, then relayed to other chains.

name: The Graph
summary: Indexing protocol that organises blockchain data into queryable APIs ("subgraphs") that apps use to read on-chain data.
goodToKnow: It reads and indexes existing chain data; unlike an oracle, it does not bring outside data on-chain.
Indexers are paid in GRT for serving queries.

name: LayerZero
summary: Cross-chain messaging protocol that lets apps on different blockchains send messages and tokens to each other.
goodToKnow: Each app chooses which verifiers (DVNs) must confirm a message, so security depends on that app's configuration.
It is a messaging layer, not a single bridge; token bridges are built on top of it. ZRO is its token.

name: Wormhole
summary: Cross-chain messaging protocol in which a set of "Guardian" validators observe and sign messages passed between blockchains.
goodToKnow: Security relies on a fixed set of 19 Guardians; a message is valid once a two-thirds majority signs it.
Its bridge was exploited in February 2022 (about 120,000 ETH-equivalent minted); the loss was covered by Jump Crypto.
W is its token; Portal is a token bridge built on Wormhole.

name: IBC
summary: Inter-Blockchain Communication: open protocol for chains to send tokens and data to each other, verified by on-chain light clients.
goodToKnow: Messages are verified by light clients of the other chain rather than a separate validator set; relayers only carry them.
Mainly used between Cosmos SDK chains, with work to connect other ecosystems.

name: EigenLayer
summary: Ethereum restaking protocol: staked ETH and other assets can be reused to secure extra services in exchange for extra rewards.
goodToKnow: Restaking adds risk: the same stake can be slashed for misbehaviour on the additional services it secures.
Its developer, Eigen Labs, now presents EigenLayer as part of a wider "EigenCloud" platform; EIGEN is the token.
Services secured this way are called AVSs (Actively Validated Services); EigenDA is one example.

name: EigenDA
summary: Data availability service secured by EigenLayer restaking, where rollups can post their transaction data instead of on Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Using external data availability lowers costs but means relying on EigenDA's operators rather than Ethereum to keep data retrievable.
It is a service built on EigenLayer, not a separate blockchain.

name: Celestia
summary: Blockchain specialised in data availability: rollups and other chains publish their transaction data on it.
goodToKnow: It is its own chain dedicated to data availability, shown with tools here.
Celestia does not execute smart contracts for those chains; it orders and stores their data and lets light nodes check it by sampling.
TIA is its native token.

name: MetaMask
summary: Self-custody wallet for Ethereum and other EVM chains, available as a browser extension and mobile app, developed by Consensys.
goodToKnow: Self-custody: whoever has the Secret Recovery Phrase controls the funds; MetaMask cannot recover it.
MetaMask staff will never ask for your recovery phrase; requests for it are scams.

name: Phantom
summary: Self-custody wallet app, originally for Solana and now supporting several other blockchains.
goodToKnow: Self-custody: whoever has the recovery phrase controls the funds; Phantom cannot recover it.

name: Safe
summary: Smart contract wallet that can require several signatures (multisig) to approve a transaction; used to hold shared funds.
goodToKnow: A Safe is a smart contract account, so it exists separately on each chain where it is deployed.
Many DAOs and teams use it to control treasuries and protocol upgrades.

name: ENS
summary: Ethereum Name Service: maps readable names such as alice.eth to wallet addresses and other data.
goodToKnow: .eth names are registered for a period and must be renewed, otherwise they can be registered by someone else.
ENS is not a DNS replacement, but some existing DNS domains can be linked to it.

name: OpenSea
summary: Marketplace for buying and selling NFTs and other tokens across several blockchains.
goodToKnow: OpenSea is a company-run interface; the NFTs themselves live on-chain, in the user's wallet, not on OpenSea.
Listing on OpenSea typically means signing an off-chain order; read signature requests carefully, as phishing often abuses them.

name: Etherscan
summary: Block explorer for Ethereum: a website to look up transactions, addresses, blocks and verified contract code.
goodToKnow: An explorer only displays public chain data; it does not hold funds and cannot reverse transactions.
Address labels and "verified" source code are Etherscan features (source is submitted by developers), not part of the chain itself.

name: Alchemy
summary: Company providing node access (RPC) and developer APIs so apps can read from and send transactions to blockchains.
goodToKnow: Many apps rely on hosted providers like Alchemy instead of running their own nodes, which concentrates infrastructure in a few companies.

name: Flashbots
summary: Research and development group behind MEV-Boost and Flashbots Protect, software that shapes how Ethereum blocks are built.
goodToKnow: MEV-Boost runs proposer-builder separation outside the protocol: validators accept full blocks from builders, through relays.
Flashbots Protect is an RPC endpoint that keeps transactions out of the public mempool, to reduce front-running.

name: OpenZeppelin
summary: Security company known for its open-source library of audited smart contract building blocks (ERC-20, ERC-721, access control).
goodToKnow: Using OpenZeppelin Contracts reduces risk but does not make a project secure by itself; custom code still needs review.
OpenZeppelin also performs smart contract security audits.

name: OP Stack
summary: Open-source software kit from Optimism for building Ethereum rollups; OP Mainnet, Unichain and Ink are built with it.
goodToKnow: A framework, not a chain: each OP Stack chain runs separately, with its own operator and settings, but shares the same core code.
As of November 2026 it is used by OP Mainnet, Unichain, Ink, World Chain, Soneium, Celo and (modified) Mantle. Base launched on it, then moved to its own node software in 2026.
OP Stack chains are optimistic rollups with fault proofs by default, but some, such as Mantle, swap in ZK validity proofs.

name: Arbitrum Orbit
summary: Offchain Labs' kit for launching custom chains on Arbitrum's Nitro software; ApeChain and Xai are built with it.
goodToKnow: As of November 2026 the official docs call these "Arbitrum chains"; "Orbit" is the earlier name, still widely used.
A chain can settle on Ethereum or on an Arbitrum L2 (making it an L3), use a custom gas token, and post data in full (Rollup) or to a committee (AnyTrust).
Degen Chain was also built with it until it shut down on 31 August 2026.

sources.label: Arbitrum docs: launch an Arbitrum chain

name: ZK Stack
summary: Matter Labs' open-source kit for building chains proven with zero-knowledge proofs; ZKsync Era is built with it.
goodToKnow: As of November 2026, chains built with it include ZKsync Era and Lens Chain. Abstract, also built with it, announced it will shut down on 15 December 2026.
A chain can be a rollup (data posted to Ethereum) or a validium (data kept elsewhere), which changes what users have to trust.
Its components include ZKsync OS and the Airbender prover; chains built with it are sometimes called the Elastic Network.

name: Cosmos SDK
summary: Open-source Go framework for building application-specific blockchains; Cosmos Hub, Osmosis and dYdX Chain use it.
goodToKnow: A toolkit, not a network: each chain built with it has its own validators and token, and can connect to others through IBC.
As of November 2026, chains built with it include Cosmos Hub, Osmosis, dYdX Chain, Celestia and Axelar. It is usually paired with CometBFT (formerly Tendermint) consensus.
"Cosmos" can mean this SDK, the Cosmos Hub chain, or the wider ecosystem of IBC-connected chains.

name: Polkadot SDK
summary: Parity's open-source Rust toolkit (formerly Substrate) for building blockchains; Polkadot itself and Avail use it.
goodToKnow: Brings Substrate, FRAME, Cumulus and the Polkadot node into one repository; chains can run on their own or connect to Polkadot.
As of November 2026, chains built with it include Polkadot, Kusama, Polkadot parachains and standalone chains such as Avail.
Building with the SDK does not by itself make a chain part of Polkadot or secured by it.

sources.label: Polkadot docs: intro to Polkadot SDK

name: Aptos
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain that runs Move smart contracts and executes transactions in parallel (Block-STM).
goodToKnow: Started by former members of Meta's Diem (Libra) project, as was Sui; both use Move, but their designs differ.
Block-STM runs transactions in parallel optimistically and re-executes those that conflict, so developers do not declare dependencies.
APT is the native token, used for fees and staking.

name: Sui
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain built around objects and the Move language, processing unrelated transactions in parallel.
goodToKnow: Assets are objects with owners; transactions that touch only their own objects can be processed in parallel with others.
Developed by Mysten Labs, founded by former Meta Diem engineers; its Move dialect differs from Aptos's.
SUI is the native token, used for gas and staking; validators reach consensus with Mysticeti, a DAG-based protocol (as of November 2026).

name: TRON
summary: Delegated proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain with an EVM-compatible virtual machine (TVM); Tether issues USDT on it.
goodToKnow: 27 elected "Super Representatives" produce blocks; TRX holders vote for them by staking.
The TVM runs Solidity contracts, but TRON addresses (starting with T), its fee model (energy and bandwidth) and tooling differ from Ethereum's.
Founded by Justin Sun; TRX is the native token.

name: TON
summary: Proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain first designed by Telegram, now run by an independent community, with its own virtual machine.
goodToKnow: Telegram dropped the project in 2020 after a US SEC lawsuit; the open-source network continued as "The Open Network", supported by the TON Foundation.
Its virtual machine (TVM) is neither the EVM nor TRON's TVM: contracts are written in languages like FunC, Tolk or Tact and talk by asynchronous messages.
Telegram's apps connect to TON (e.g. wallets and Mini Apps), but Telegram does not run the network.

name: NEAR
summary: Sharded proof-of-stake layer-1 blockchain whose smart contracts compile to WebAssembly, usually written in Rust or JavaScript.
goodToKnow: Nightshade sharding splits the network into shards that process transactions in parallel; accounts have readable names like alice.near.
Not EVM-native: Ethereum tools do not work directly; an EVM environment (Aurora) runs as a separate project on top of NEAR.
Chain Signatures let NEAR accounts sign transactions on other blockchains (as of November 2026).

name: Hyperliquid
summary: Layer-1 blockchain built for trading: on-chain order books (HyperCore) plus an EVM smart-contract layer (HyperEVM).
goodToKnow: HyperCore and HyperEVM are two parts of one chain, both secured by HyperBFT, a HotStuff-inspired proof-of-stake consensus (as of November 2026).
It has a much smaller validator set than Ethereum, which helps speed but concentrates control in fewer hands.
HYPE is the native token, used for gas and staking. Hyperliquid is its own L1, not an Ethereum L2 or rollup.

name: Polygon PoS
summary: Proof-of-stake EVM chain that regularly checkpoints its state to Ethereum; often called a sidechain rather than a rollup.
goodToKnow: Its own validators secure it: Ethereum stores checkpoints but does not verify each transaction, so it does not inherit Ethereum's security like a rollup.
POL replaced MATIC as the gas and staking token in September 2024; most MATIC has since been migrated to POL.
Hard forks in 2025–2026 (e.g. Heimdall v2, Rio, Giugliano) aimed at faster finality; as of November 2026 it remains a PoS chain, not a rollup.

sources.label: Polygon blog: MATIC to POL migration

name: Zcash
summary: Proof-of-work cryptocurrency that adds optional private (shielded) transactions using zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs).
goodToKnow: Privacy is optional: transparent addresses work like Bitcoin's; only shielded transactions hide sender, receiver and amount.
Launched in 2016 from a fork of Bitcoin's code; ZEC is the native coin.
Crosslink, a proposed hybrid of proof of work and proof of stake, is being tested but is not active on mainnet as of November 2026.

name: Stacks
summary: Smart-contract network anchored to Bitcoin through Proof of Transfer; it calls itself a Bitcoin L2, a label some dispute.
goodToKnow: Proof of Transfer: miners spend BTC to win Stacks blocks, and STX holders who lock ("stack") tokens can earn that BTC; blocks are anchored in Bitcoin transactions.
Critics call it a separate chain rather than a true L2: it has its own token (STX) and consensus, and Bitcoin does not verify its transactions.
Contracts use the Clarity language; sBTC is a 1:1 BTC-backed asset on Stacks, managed by a set of signers.

name: Rootstock
summary: EVM-compatible sidechain merge-mined with Bitcoin, using a two-way peg (PowPeg) that locks BTC to issue RBTC.
goodToKnow: Often marketed as a "Bitcoin L2", but many classify it as a sidechain: it has its own consensus, and the peg relies on a federation of signers.
Bitcoin miners can mine it at the same time (merged mining), so it reuses Bitcoin's hash power without extra energy.
RBTC, pegged 1:1 to BTC, pays fees; PowPeg signers keep their keys in hardware security modules.

name: Unichain
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup on the OP Stack, launched by Uniswap Labs for DeFi and fast trading.
goodToKnow: The Uniswap protocol runs on many chains; Unichain is a separate network that Uniswap Labs launched (mainnet February 2025).
Like other OP Stack chains, withdrawals to Ethereum rely on fault proofs and a challenge period (as of November 2026).
Blocks are built inside a TEE and streamed as sub-second "Flashblocks" preconfirmations; final settlement still happens on Ethereum.

name: Mantle
summary: Ethereum rollup on a modified OP Stack that uses ZK validity proofs (OP Succinct) and posts its data to Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Started as an optimistic rollup; since September 2025 OP Succinct ZK proofs (SP1) validate its state, shortening withdrawals from about 7 days.
Data availability: Mantle used EigenDA from 2025, then moved to Ethereum blobs; its April 2026 Arsia upgrade removed EigenDA (as of November 2026).
MNT is the gas token; Mantle grew out of the BitDAO community.

name: Taiko
summary: Ethereum-equivalent "based" rollup: blocks are ordered via Ethereum L1 and proven with several proofs, including ZK.
goodToKnow: "Based" means Ethereum L1 handles sequencing; as of November 2026, fast proposing is limited to whitelisted preconfirmers, with forced inclusion as a fallback.
Multi-proof: since the 2026 Unzen fork, each proven range needs two proofs from SGX (TEE), SP1 or RISC0, at least one of them a ZK proof.
The mainnet is called Taiko Alethia; ETH pays gas and TAIKO is the project's token.

name: Ink
summary: Ethereum optimistic rollup on the OP Stack, launched by the Kraken exchange.
goodToKnow: Ink is separate from Kraken's exchange: funds on Ink are in a self-custody wallet, not in a Kraken account balance.
Like other OP Stack chains, withdrawals to Ethereum rely on fault proofs and a challenge period (as of November 2026).
Mainnet launched in December 2024; it is one of the OP Stack chains in Optimism's Superchain.

name: Aztec
summary: Privacy-focused Ethereum ZK rollup whose smart contracts can keep balances and data private, with proofs made on users' devices.
goodToKnow: As of November 2026 mainnet is in "Alpha": live with staking and user transactions, but called early, unaudited software. V6 ("Tierra") shipped in November 2026.
Contracts are written in Aztec.nr, based on the Noir language, not Solidity; it is not EVM-compatible.
Not the same as Aztec Connect, an earlier Aztec rollup that was shut down in 2024.

name: Degen Chain
summary: An Arbitrum Orbit L3 that settled on Base and used DEGEN for gas; it shut down on 31 August 2026.
goodToKnow: Kept on the map as an example: chains can shut down, and users must move assets off before bridges and RPC services are switched off.
The DEGEN token lives on Base and continues; the team wound down the chain to focus on social products in the Base ecosystem.
It had multi-day outages in 2024, a known risk for small chains that rely on a single operator.

name: Compound
summary: Lending protocol where users supply crypto to earn interest and borrow against collateral, governed by COMP holders.
goodToKnow: The current version, Compound III ("Comet"), runs separate markets that each lend one base asset such as USDC, unlike v2's shared pools.
Loans are overcollateralised: if collateral value falls too far, the position is liquidated.
cTokens belong to the older Compound v2; v3 is deployed on Ethereum and several L2s (as of November 2026).

name: Morpho
summary: Lending protocol made of isolated, permissionless markets, plus curated vaults that spread deposits across them.
goodToKnow: Each market pairs one collateral asset with one loan asset and fixed parameters, so risk stays isolated rather than pooled.
Vaults are managed by third-party curators who choose the markets; depositors take on the curator's risk choices.
Began as an optimiser on top of Aave and Compound before launching its own markets (Morpho Blue) in 2024; MORPHO is the governance token.

name: Pendle
summary: DeFi protocol that splits yield-bearing tokens into principal (PT) and yield (YT) tokens so future yield can be traded.
goodToKnow: Buying PT locks in a fixed yield until maturity; buying YT is a bet that the variable yield will be higher.
Users take on the underlying asset's risks plus smart-contract risk; YT is worth nothing after maturity.
PENDLE is the protocol's token; it is deployed on Ethereum and several other chains.

name: Raydium
summary: Decentralised exchange on Solana that uses automated market makers (AMMs) for token swaps and liquidity pools.
goodToKnow: Offers standard constant-product pools and concentrated-liquidity pools; aggregators such as Jupiter often route trades through it.
Its LaunchLab lets anyone create and launch tokens; newly launched tokens carry high risk.
RAY is the protocol token.

name: Jito
summary: Solana project offering the JitoSOL liquid-staking token and MEV infrastructure (a validator client and block engine).
goodToKnow: Its validator client lets searchers pay tips to get transaction bundles included; tips are shared with validators and their stakers.
JitoSOL represents staked SOL plus staking and MEV rewards; it carries smart-contract and validator risks.
JTO is the governance token; critics note that Jito's block engine concentrates part of Solana's MEV flow.

sources.label: Jito Labs docs: low-latency transaction send

name: Binance
summary: Centralised, custodial cryptocurrency exchange for trading, depositing and withdrawing crypto across many blockchains.
goodToKnow: Custodial: Binance holds users' keys, so funds there are an account balance, not self-custody.
BNB Chain grew out of Binance and BNB is that chain's token; the exchange and the chain are separate things.
In 2023 Binance and founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in the US to anti-money-laundering violations; he was pardoned in October 2025.

name: Ethena (USDe)
summary: Protocol issuing USDe, a synthetic dollar backed by crypto hedged with short futures, not a fiat-backed stablecoin.
goodToKnow: Core design: crypto such as ETH or BTC is paired with short perpetual/futures positions (delta-neutral). USDe is not backed by dollars in a bank.
As of November 2026 much of the backing has shifted to lending, stablecoins and tokenised assets; the mix changes over time and by governance.
Risks include negative funding rates, exchange or custodian failure and liquidity; sUSDe is the staked, yield-bearing version.

name: PYUSD (PayPal)
summary: US-dollar stablecoin issued by Paxos for PayPal, redeemable 1:1 and backed by dollar deposits and short-term US Treasuries.
goodToKnow: Paxos issues it and holds the reserves; PayPal brands it and offers it in its apps (launched August 2023).
Issued natively on Ethereum, Solana and other chains (as of November 2026); bridged versions on other chains are different tokens.
Centrally issued: the issuer can freeze tokens held at specific addresses.

name: EURC (Circle)
summary: Euro stablecoin issued by Circle, redeemable 1:1 for euros and backed by euro-denominated reserves.
goodToKnow: Issued under the EU's MiCA rules by Circle's French entity (as of November 2026); it was formerly called Euro Coin (EUROC).
Issued natively on Ethereum, Solana, Avalanche, Base and other chains; it is a separate token from USDC.
Centrally issued: Circle can freeze tokens held at specific addresses.

sources.label: Circle developer docs: what is EURC

name: Ledger
summary: Company making hardware wallets: devices that keep private keys offline and sign transactions for many blockchains.
goodToKnow: The device holds the keys; the Ledger Wallet app (formerly Ledger Live) or wallets like MetaMask show balances and prepare transactions.
Anyone with the 24-word recovery phrase can take the funds; Ledger never asks for it.
A 2020 customer-database leak exposed buyers' contact details and led to phishing; it did not expose keys.

name: Trust Wallet
summary: Self-custody mobile and browser wallet for many blockchains, owned by Binance.
goodToKnow: Self-custody: keys stay on the user's device, so losing the recovery phrase means losing access.
Owned by Binance since 2018, but funds in Trust Wallet sit on-chain in the user's addresses, not in a Binance account.
In December 2025 a malicious Chrome extension update (v2.68) drained some users' wallets; the mobile app was not affected.

sources.label: Trust Wallet: v2.68 extension incident update

name: Polymarket
summary: Prediction market where users trade shares on the outcome of real-world events, settled in USDC on Polygon PoS.
goodToKnow: Prices reflect traders' bets, not certainties; markets are resolved through UMA's optimistic oracle, and some outcomes have been disputed.
Access depends on the country; in the US it runs a separate, CFTC-regulated platform (as of November 2026).
As of November 2026 it runs on Polygon PoS; it has said it plans to move to another chain.

name: Farcaster
summary: Decentralised social network protocol: accounts are registered on-chain and posts are stored on its own network (Snapchain).
goodToKnow: Account IDs (FIDs) are registered in contracts on OP Mainnet; posts and other messages are kept off Ethereum on Snapchain.
Many apps (clients) can read the same accounts and posts; the main app was formerly called Warpcast.
Ownership changed twice in 2026: Neynar acquired it in January, then Network School in October (as of November 2026).

name: Infura
summary: Hosted node service from Consensys that lets apps and wallets read and send blockchain data without running their own nodes.
goodToKnow: MetaMask uses Infura by default for many networks, so an Infura outage or policy change can affect MetaMask users.
Using a provider means trusting it for correct data and uptime; it can also see request metadata such as IP addresses.
As of November 2026 its documentation is published under MetaMask's developer services.

name: Hardhat
summary: Development environment for compiling, testing, deploying and debugging Ethereum smart contracts, built in TypeScript.
goodToKnow: Runs a local Ethereum network for testing; tests are often written in TypeScript, and Hardhat 3 also supports tests written in Solidity.
Maintained by the Nomic Foundation, a non-profit.
A developer tool, not a blockchain or a wallet; it is often compared with Foundry.

name: Foundry
summary: Command-line toolkit written in Rust for building, testing and deploying EVM smart contracts, with tests written in Solidity.
goodToKnow: Includes forge (build and test), cast (interact with chains), anvil (local node) and chisel (Solidity shell).
Tests, including fuzz tests, are written in Solidity itself; it is often compared with Hardhat.
Open source, started at Paradigm; version 1.0 was released in 2025.

name: Chronicle
summary: Oracle network that grew out of MakerDAO's oracle team; it supplies price feeds to Sky (formerly MakerDAO) and others.
goodToKnow: Its Scribe oracle contracts use Schnorr signatures so many validators' signatures can be checked cheaply on-chain.
Feeds are signed by a known set of validators (e.g. Bitcoin Suisse, Steakhouse Financial), so users trust that group.
Reading many feeds requires being whitelisted; it also offers proof-of-asset data for tokenised real-world assets (as of November 2026).

name: RedStone
summary: Modular oracle that delivers signed price data to many chains, either pushed on-chain or pulled into transactions on demand.
goodToKnow: Pull model: prices are signed off-chain and attached to the user's transaction, which saves gas but needs app integration.
Provides feeds for newer assets such as liquid-restaking tokens; RED is its token (as of November 2026).
Any oracle means trusting its data providers and signers: wrong prices can trigger wrong liquidations.

name: Dune
summary: Analytics platform where people query indexed blockchain data with SQL and share dashboards.
goodToKnow: Dashboards are made by users; each query has its own assumptions, so the same metric can differ between dashboards.
Data from many chains is decoded and indexed; free use has limits, and an API is available.
An analytics tool, not an oracle: smart contracts cannot read Dune data directly.

name: Arkham
summary: Blockchain analytics platform that labels addresses with real-world entities and lets users track fund flows.
goodToKnow: Labels come from its own analysis and user submissions; attributions can be wrong and should be double-checked.
Its "Intel Exchange" lets users post bounties for identifying addresses, which raised privacy concerns.
Arkham also launched a crypto exchange in 2024; in February 2026 it was reported to be winding down, which Arkham called a move to a DEX.

name: Chainalysis
summary: Blockchain analytics company whose tools trace funds and flag risky addresses for governments, exchanges and investigators.
goodToKnow: Its software (e.g. Reactor, KYT) is used for compliance and law-enforcement investigations, such as tracing stolen funds.
Attribution relies on clustering heuristics and intelligence; it is powerful but not infallible, and its methods have been challenged in court.
A private company, not a protocol and without a token.

name: Axelar
summary: Cross-chain network with its own proof-of-stake validators that passes messages and tokens between blockchains.
goodToKnow: Built with the Cosmos SDK; its validators jointly sign cross-chain messages, so security depends on that validator set.
Offers general message passing (GMP) and an Interchain Token Service; AXL is the staking token.
Circle agreed in December 2025 to acquire the Interop Labs team; the network and AXL stayed independent, with Common Prefix taking a lead role.

sources.label: Circle: agreement to acquire Interop Labs team

name: Across
summary: Intent-based bridge where relayers front funds on the destination chain and are repaid later after verification.
goodToKnow: Users receive funds quickly because a relayer pays them up front; relayers carry the delay and risk until they are repaid.
Repayments are checked through UMA's optimistic oracle, which can be disputed during a challenge window.
ACX is the protocol token; it moves assets mainly between Ethereum, its L2s and other chains.

name: Hyperlane
summary: Permissionless interoperability protocol: anyone can deploy it to a chain and send messages and tokens between chains.
goodToKnow: Each app chooses its own security setup (Interchain Security Modules), so safety varies from one deployment to another.
Warp Routes move tokens between chains, using lock-and-mint or burn-and-mint designs.
Formerly called Abacus; HYPER is its token (launched 2025).

name: CCTP (Circle)
summary: Circle's Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol: it burns USDC on one chain and mints native USDC on another, with no wrapped tokens.
goodToKnow: Circle signs an attestation for each burn, so users trust Circle, the USDC issuer, rather than a third-party bridge.
CCTP V2 adds faster transfers and hooks; the older V1 is being deprecated, with a full pause scheduled for 1 December 2026.
It only moves Circle-issued tokens such as USDC, not arbitrary assets.

name: ether.fi
summary: Liquid restaking protocol: users stake ETH, receive eETH or weETH, and the ETH is restaked through EigenLayer.
goodToKnow: The liquid tokens keep staked ETH usable in DeFi, but add smart-contract, slashing and depeg risks on top of staking.
Also offers a crypto-backed payment card and other "neobank" products (as of November 2026).
ETHFI is the governance token.

name: Symbiotic
summary: Permissionless restaking protocol on Ethereum where networks can be secured by many kinds of staked ERC-20 collateral.
goodToKnow: Unlike EigenLayer's ETH-first start, it accepts many ERC-20 assets as collateral, with vaults setting their own rules.
Restaked collateral can be slashed if operators misbehave, adding risk on top of the asset's own risks.
Networks that use it for "shared security" pay operators and stakers rewards in return.

name: Avail
summary: Data availability blockchain, built with the Polkadot SDK, where rollups can publish their data instead of on Ethereum.
goodToKnow: Uses KZG commitments and data availability sampling, so light clients can check that data was published without downloading all of it.
Spun out of Polygon in 2023; AVAIL is its staking token.
Rollups using it rely on Avail's validators, not Ethereum, to keep their data available.

name: Railgun
summary: Privacy system on EVM chains that lets users hold and use tokens in a shielded balance, using zero-knowledge proofs.
goodToKnow: Runs as smart contracts on Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum and BNB Chain; it is not a separate blockchain.
"Private Proofs of Innocence" aim to keep funds from known illicit sources out of the shielded pool.
It does not guarantee anonymity: timing and amounts can still link transactions.
